Photograph: Sarah Meyssonnier/Reuters View image in fullscreen The response from police has been heavy-handed but it has not stopped the waves of protests from growing. Photograph: Sarah Meyssonnier/Reuters This Is Europe World news France’s students are angry about more than crumbling classrooms and missing teachers Beneath a wave of school protests in France lies a more existential worry: the future prospects of an entire generation Don’t get This Is Europe delivered to your inbox? Sign up here Jon Henley Europe correspondent Wed 14 Oct 2026 10.29 EDT Last modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 10.34 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Say what you will about France’s high schools, they still produce world-class slogan writers. Here’s a brief selection spotted during three weeks of blockades and marches over chronic teacher shortages, overcrowded classes and crumbling buildings: “ Pas d’avenir, pas de calme ” (No future, no calm). “ Diplômés aujourd’hui, précaires demain ” (Graduates today, insecure tomorrow). “ Vous détruisez notre futur, on bloque votre présent ” (You destroy our future, we block your present). A couple more: “ Nos lycées tombent en ruines, comme nos espoirs ” (Our schools, like our hopes, are falling into ruin”). “ On n’est pas mal éduqués, on n’est pas écoutés ” (We’re not badly brought up, we’re just not being listened to). Spot the common theme? The protests, which continued this week with more than 160,000 on the streets on Tuesday, might be over very material problems – but beneath them there clearly lies an altogether more existential worry. This generation fears its future will be one of diminishing prospects, poorly paid, unstable jobs, unaffordable living costs and steadily decaying public infrastructure – the end, in short, of the basic socioeconomic security their parents, mostly, enjoyed. That was the central theme of a 30-second Instagram post I recorded last week with the Guardian’s social media team and that, at time of writing, had been watched almost 540,000 times – with young people in France the largest single group of viewers. The same core concerns underlie youth protests elsewhere – notably, ongoing mass housing demonstrations in Spain , where the twentysomethings of Madrid and Barcelona are in revolt at the monthly rental on a one-bed flat costing an entire monthly median salary. In France, teenagers in Seine-Saint-Denis , a low-income area in the north of Paris, show reporters pictures of broken chairs and desks, holes in walls, leaking ceilings, mould, shattered toilets and defective audiovisual equipment. Some have gone months without key teachers. The consequence, here, is protest. As Kitty Sayers, who went to school in France, explained , France’s republic “was born of insurrection and has never forgotten it … The language of rights, citizenship and collective power is woven into French education.” This means that in French schools protest is “taught as a legally framed, fundamental right and a civic responsibility”. But the government’s response has also been arguably very French: riot police, teargas, baton charges and stun grenades. More than 250 pupils have been injured, along with about 100 school staff and 750 police. One teen has lost a hand from a stun grenade, another the sight in one eye, a third his teeth. More than 6,000 people – almost all minors – have been detained. After a public outcry, the interior minister last week suspended the use of stun grenades . But as Alexander Hurst observed , when pupils complain about the state of their schools “and the response is riot police, the government has lost the plot”. Wider public support View image in fullscreen ‘Hands off our children’ … there is widespread support for the protests. Photograph: Sarah Meyssonnier/Reuters If the government hoped public opinion would be on its side, it miscalculated. Teachers’ and other unions, parents and university students have marched with the pupils, and a poll this week showed 57% of the public approved of the protests, with 33% opposed. They come at a particularly delicate time for France’s political establishment. Presidential elections to replace Emmanuel Macron are due next spring, and without a parliamentary majority his government is caught in legislative deadlock. Meanwhile, Marine Le Pen’s far-right National Rally and the radical-left La France Insoumise of Jean-Luc Mélenchon are weaponising the protests, the former castigating an out-of-control youth, the latter an out-of-control police, and both blaming centrist incompetence. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion Above all, the government’s financial room for manoeuvre is all but nonexistent. As Philip Inman pointed out , with a debt-to-GDP ratio and a budget deficit both among the highest in the EU, France has no cash to spare – and the markets are watching. So while cost-cutting will only provoke more unrest, the absence of it could trigger a boycott of French bonds, or even a default and bailout (although as the economist Paul Krugman says , France “may have crossed from too big to fail to too big to save”). Ultimately, there seems little doubt France will have to make some of the same painful adjustments to bring its debt back under control that Italy, Spain and Greece made a decade or more ago – and to which French public reaction could be dramatic. We began with slogans; let’s end with some. The best-known French youth protest – a revolution, more or less – was, of course, May 1968. Comparing its iconic posters with those of today’s demonstrating school pupils is instructive. In 1968, there was “ Sous les pavés, la plage ” (Beneath the cobblestones, the beach); “ L’imagination au pouvoir ” (Put imagination in charge); “L’ennui est contre-révolutionnaire” (Boredom is counter-revolutionary). Those, you can see, were slogans born out of infinite possibility: a generation that, in overthrowing the old social hierarchies, never doubted its material survival. May 68 was about blowing open the doors of a rigid, outmoded society to grasp a bright future. Today’s students are fighting to stop the doors slamming shut on them altogether. http://www.bgnes.com/no-filter/four-refe.text: BGNES Opinion Four Referendums Deepen Slovenia’s Political Divide Ahead of Elections Four Referendums Deepen Slovenia’s Political Divide Ahead of Elections 09.10.2026 - 17:52 Share BGNES The outcome could influence debates over the limits of state authority, social responsibility, media independence and the relationship between citizenship and democratic participation. Around 1.7 million Slovenian voters will cast their ballots on Sunday, October 11, in four referendums that have become a test of the country's widening political divide. The votes concern the participation of non-EU citizens in local elections, the conditions attached to social assistance, the funding of public broadcasting and the powers of parliamentary investigative commissions. Although each proposal addresses a different area of public policy, the campaign has largely been shaped by the confrontation between the conservative camp led by Janez Jansa and the governing left. The two sides have adopted opposing positions across the board. The conservative bloc, which includes the Slovenian Democratic Party (SDS), New Slovenia (NSi), Anze Logar's Democrats, the Slovenian People's Party and Marko Lotric's Focus party, is urging voters to support all four proposals. The governing coalition, comprising the Freedom Movement, the Social Democrats and Levica, is campaigning for four "no" votes. The outcome could influence debates over the limits of state authority, social responsibility, media independence and the relationship between citizenship and democratic participation. Parliamentary oversight at the centre of the dispute The referendum with the most direct legislative consequences concerns a law on parliamentary investigative commissions adopted in May. The initiative came from the opposition and left-leaning civil society groups, whom conservatives accuse of operating as political movements under the guise of non-governmental organisations. At the heart of the dispute is the extent to which parliamentary commissions should be able to investigate suspected wrongdoing. A reform introduced in 2024 by then-parliamentary speaker Urska Klakocar Zupancic established legal safeguards intended to prevent hearings from becoming what its supporters called a "political circus". The new law restores elements of the original 1993 framework, which remained in force for 31 years. Its supporters on the right argue that the changes would remove barriers to corruption investigations. Janez Jakel, an MP from New Slovenia, told Slovenian media that the 2024 reform had been designed by the previous centre-left government to protect Prime Minister Robert Golob personally and obstruct inquiries into financial flows at the energy group GEN-I, which Golob led before entering government. Conservatives have also cited the arrest in Romania of Gasper Hudohmet, director of GEN-I Sonce, a subsidiary of the group and an associate of Golob. Hudohmet is accused of soliciting a €450,000 bribe in connection with a major energy contract. The right has additionally revived allegations made shortly before the 2022 elections concerning a purported Romanian bank account in Golob's name, arguing that the matter has never been adequately explained. Other controversies have reinforced the opposition's criticism of the government. These include the purchase of a building on Litijska Street for €7.7 million in public funds by former Justice Minister Dominika Svarc Pipan of the Social Democrats. The transaction drew widespread criticism. Another disputed case involved 13,000 computers purchased by the state for its poorest citizens but left in storage for years without being distributed. Investigations involving Ljubljana Mayor Zoran Jankovic have also fuelled questions about public accountability. The left and several non-governmental organisations warn that the new law could create a form of "political police". They argue that it removes the possibility of immediate appeals to the Constitutional Court and could give MPs access to private information without independent oversight, including bank accounts and personal data belonging to ordinary citizens, business owners and public officials. The controversy has also prompted accusations that state institutions are being used for political purposes. Conservatives have criticised Tamara Vonta of the Freedom Movement, who chairs parliamentary investigative commissions. A group of businesspeople has filed a criminal complaint against her, accusing her of abuse of office and violating financial confidentiality. The central question is whether parliamentary inquiries can be given sufficient powers to investigate suspected corruption without exposing individuals to politically motivated scrutiny. Welfare policy divides voters over work obligations Another referendum asks voters whether access to social assistance should be made conditional on performing community service, such as maintaining public green spaces. The vote is advisory rather than legally binding. The scheme costs approximately €20 million a month and supports around 67,000 people. A single person currently receives a basic monthly benefit of €507.43. Conservatives argue that the proposal is justified by historically low unemployment and a substantial shortage of workers. Employers have filled some vacancies with workers from the Balkans and Asia. Given the number of available jobs, the right questions why some people receiving benefits should not be required to contribute through work. Left-wing organisations and experts interpret the same labour market conditions differently. They argue that if jobs are so readily available, most people capable of working have already found employment. Those who continue to rely on assistance may face more complex barriers, including health problems, extreme poverty or partial disability. Compulsory community service could therefore impose additional demands on people already living in difficult circumstances. The debate goes beyond the proposed scheme itself. It raises a broader question about the purpose of social protection: whether benefits should be more closely linked to reciprocal obligations or remain a safety net for people whose circumstances may prevent them from finding work. Public broadcaster's funding under scrutiny The proposed abolition of the mandatory licence fee for Slovenian Radio and Television (RTV SLO) is the subject of a third advisory referendum. The fee currently amounts to approximately €170 a year. The right accuses the public broadcaster of consistently favouring left-wing political views. Jansa and his allies have repeatedly boycotted its journalists. Recent figures from RTV SLO show that representatives of the governing majority failed to respond to more than 40 invitations to appear on its programmes during the preceding 30 days. Opponents of abolishing the fee, including prominent figures from the cultural sector aligned with the left, have described the proposal as a "suicidal act". They warn that removing the existing funding mechanism would deprive the broadcaster of a stable source of revenue, potentially leaving it vulnerable to political interference or the influence of private capital. The debate also reflects wider European discussions about how public-service media should be financed. Some voters are seeking information about models used in 14 other countries, including France, where public broadcasters receive direct funding from the state budget. For both sides, the issue extends beyond the cost of maintaining the broadcaster. Supporters of abolition are challenging the current funding system, while opponents fear that changing it could undermine the institution's independence and make it more susceptible to political pressure. Voting rights for non-EU residents spark sovereignty debate The fourth referendum concerns the right of citizens from outside the European Union to vote in Slovenian local elections. Analysts have viewed the measure as part of a wider shift towards a more sovereigntist political agenda. Earlier this summer, the governing coalition removed the voting right from more than 103,000 non-EU nationals holding permanent residence in Slovenia. EU citizens are unaffected by the change. Since the right was introduced in 2002, the number of people covered by it has increased tenfold, from approximately 10,000 to more than 103,000, largely as a result of immigration from the Western Balkans. Conservatives maintain that people who are not Slovenian citizens should not be able to influence political balances in the country's municipalities. The issue has attracted particular attention in Ljubljana, where non-EU residents account for between 10% and 12% of the population. Similar proportions have been reported in Maribor, Celje and Velenje. Conservative politicians in the capital are concerned that non-EU residents could provide substantial electoral support for incumbent Mayor Zoran Jankovic, whose administration has faced corruption investigations. Anze Logar's Democrats have also invoked reciprocity, pointing out that Slovenian citizens living abroad cannot vote in local elections in Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina or Kosovo. The opposition has denounced the restriction as xenophobic and criticised the abrupt removal of a right that had existed for nearly a quarter of a century. It argues that long-term foreign residents are part of Slovenian society, describing them as "our friends" who have lived, worked and paid taxes in the country for decades. Slovenia generally does not permit dual citizenship, adding another dimension to the debate over political participation. The dispute reflects two competing views of democratic representation: whether local voting rights should be reserved exclusively for citizens or should also take account of the contributions of people who have established permanent lives in the country. Warnings over Slovenia's political direction The four referendums are taking place against a backdrop of increasingly polarised political debate, with opinion polls suggesting the possibility of a right-wing victory. The left has stepped up its warnings about the country's future. Former Prime Minister Robert Golob told the daily Vecer that Slovenia risked moving towards a "police state" and a "form of dictatorship". Political scientist Igor Luksic, a lecturer at the Faculty of Social Sciences and former leader of the Social Democrats, has urged caution in assessing such claims. Speaking to Info 360, he said there was not yet sufficient objective evidence to conclude that Slovenia was moving in that direction. He argued that there was no concrete proof of an authoritarian shift by the government and noted that public opinion did not generally view the situation in such alarming terms. Jansa, meanwhile, has maintained a more restrained public profile than during his previous terms in office and has remained relatively quiet. Taken together, the four votes highlight the competing priorities at the heart of Slovenia's political debate. The proposed changes to parliamentary investigations have become a proxy for disputes over corruption and institutional safeguards. The social assistance referendum tests competing views on welfare and employment, while the public broadcasting vote raises questions about financial independence and political influence. The restrictions on local voting rights for non-EU nationals, in turn, place citizenship and national sovereignty at the centre of the discussion. Despite their different subject matter, the campaigns have increasingly been framed around opposing political identities rather than the merits of each individual proposal. The recurring "us versus them" narrative illustrates the depth of the divide as Slovenia approaches another consequential political test. | BGNES Follow us also on Watch and Comment news Comment in X More from Opinion Eight Ships in 18 Days: Series of Attacks off Bulgaria and Romania Undermines Black Sea Security 23.10.2026 - https://www.hindustantimes.com/world-new.text: US Ambassador to Poland Tom Rose, on October 31, urged officials, police and protesters to avoid escalation amid the political crisis regarding Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal. The rival sides have accused each other of undermining democratic institutions.Rose said the confrontation represented an “unprecedented” dispute over the government’s use of state power and the independence of a key constitutional body. He called on all parties to “take a deep breath” and avoid actions that could trigger violence.Thousands have gathered outside the Constitutional Tribunal in Warsaw amid a growing dispute between supporters of Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s government and opponents who accused authorities of attempting to weaken the judiciary. Poland's constitutional court in a social media post described the scenario by writing, “All persons participating in these actions are committing the crime of a coup d'etat.”Also read: Polish President's mid-air U-turn, riot police at court, street protests: Poland's top court crisis deepens Washington calls for dialogue as Poland faces political tensionsThe United States has closely watched developments in Poland because of the country’s strategic role in Europe. Poland is a key NATO member and a major supporter of Ukraine amid Russia’s war.Rose said Poland’s democratic strength must come from its own citizens and institutions. He called on political leaders to protect the rule of law and avoid actions that could damage public trust.“Both sides offer sharply different accounts of what happened and why. Whatever the facts ultimately establish, thousands gathering outside the Tribunal make an already dangerous situation more combustible. The last thing Poland needs is a confrontation that spirals into something far worse,” Rose wrote.He further added, “America is on Poland’s side. It is not our place to judge or interfere in its internal affairs. Our concern is for the stability, security, and democratic future of a country we are proud to call our friend and ally.”“Poland has come too far and accomplished too much to let political differences, no matter how strongly felt, put any of that at risk,” Rose wrote.Also read: Poland opposition accuses Tusk government of 'coup' as police surround top courtGovernment and opposition clash over tribunal authorityThe crisis centres on a dispute over Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal, one of the country’s highest judicial bodies. The tribunal has been at the centre of years of political conflict involving judicial reforms, appointments and questions over institutional independence.Supporters of Tusk’s government argue that previous changes made under the former conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government weakened judicial independence. They said that reforms are needed to restore confidence in state institutions and align Poland with European Union standards.Opponents accused the government of using state power to remove judges and challenge institutions that do not support its agenda. They argue that actions against the tribunal threaten constitutional checks and balances.The dispute has created a tense atmosphere outside the tribunal, where protestors are gathered. Rose warned that large crowds could make an already sensitive situation more dangerous. “Thousands gathering outside the Tribunal make an already dangerous situation more combustible,” Rose said. He urged government officials, law enforcement and protesters to avoid any action that could “provoke violence or further escalation.” (This story is being updated)
